opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the joy comes from a few places at once.

The first is just the math itself. I've loved math since I was a kid, and there's a specific feeling when a proof finally clicks, when something that seemed impossibly tangled suddenly becomes inevitable. What's thrilling about AI for math is that we're trying to build systems that can have something like that moment too, and maybe help humans have it more often. So it doesn't feel like I left math to do a startup. It feels like I'm doing math at a different level of abstraction.

The second is that math is such a clean testing ground for intelligence. With formal verification, using languages like Lean, you get a ground truth that's incredibly rare in AI. A proof either checks or it doesn't. There's no arguing with the reward signal, no vibes-based evaluation. That honesty is really satisfying. When our system makes progress, we *know* it made progress. I find that deeply reassuring in a field where a lot of claims are hard to verify.

The third is the people. At Axiom we have this mix of mathematicians, AI researchers, and people who've built programming languages and compilers, and watching them teach each other is one of the most fun parts of my day. A mathematician will explain why a certain lemma is "obviously" true, and an engineer will ask, "Okay, but how would a machine know that's obvious?" Those conversations end up revealing things about mathematics that nobody had written down before.

And finally, there's the sense that we're early. It feels a bit like being in the room when a new field is forming. The idea that within our lifetimes we might have an AI mathematician that can generate conjectures, prove them, and verify them, and that this could eventually feed into things like verified software and science more broadly, is a very big dream. Getting to work on a big dream every day, with people I respect, while still doing the thing I loved as a kid — I don't know what else you'd call that but joyful.

r001.rationale: The response attributes joy to the math, formal verification, team discussions, and the sense of working on an early field. It does not say that Carina enjoys working with authors of AI-for-Math papers she had previously read.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, the joy comes from a few different places, and they're kind of layered on top of each other.

The first is just the math itself. I fell in love with mathematics as a kid because it's the one domain where you can be completely certain about something. When you prove a theorem, it's true forever, in every universe, independent of who you are or when you lived. There's a kind of purity to that which I've never found anywhere else. So getting to spend my days thinking about how machines can participate in that, how they can discover and verify mathematical truth, that's a privilege in itself.

The second layer is the people. Axiom is a small team, and a lot of us came from the olympiad world or from research mathematics, and then found our way into AI. When you put people like that in a room, the conversations are incredibly fun. Someone will be arguing about a formalization choice in Lean, and ten minutes later the same conversation turns into a debate about what it even means for a proof to be "understood." I learn something every day, and I don't think most jobs give you that.

And the third thing, which I think is the deepest, is the sense that this is actually possible now. For a long time, "AI that does math" was a kind of science-fiction aspiration. Now we have models that can produce complete formal proofs, we have verification systems that can check them with zero ambiguity, and the gap between the two is closing fast. There's a very specific feeling when you're working on something that was impossible five years ago and is going to look obvious in five more years. You feel like you're standing at exactly the right moment.

I'd also say, and this might sound a bit sentimental, that mathematics has always been a deeply human endeavor, built on the shoulders of people like Euler and Gauss and Noether. The idea that we might expand who, or what, can contribute to that tradition, and in doing so help human mathematicians reach further than they otherwise could, is something I find genuinely moving. Not replacing mathematicians, but giving them a new kind of collaborator. That's what gets me out of bed.

astra-6.text:
For me, the joy is in discovery. With mathematics, you can spend a long time feeling stuck, and then one idea makes everything click. Working on AI for math brings another layer to that: can we build something that helps us find those ideas, or see a problem in a way we wouldn’t have on our own?

And there’s joy in sharing that process. You get to think about difficult questions with people who are excited by them, trade ideas, and learn together. Even when the progress is small, that makes the work rewarding.
